summary.text: Quantum entanglement is when the quantum state of each particle in a group cannot be described independently of the others, even across a large distance.
Measurements on entangled particles can be perfectly correlated, yet individual outcomes cannot be controlled, so entanglement cannot send faster-than-light messages.
Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen raised it as a paradox in 1935, and later tests of Bell's inequality showed no local hidden variables can explain it.

facts.value: Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen published their paradox in 1935

facts.value: Schrödinger used the German word Verschränkung, translated as entanglement

facts.value: Proposed in 1992 and realized experimentally in 1997

items.prompt: Two particles are created with total spin zero. You find one spinning clockwise on an axis. What will you find for the other on the same axis?

options.label: Also clockwise, so the total doubles
A random direction unrelated to the first
No spin at all
Counterclockwise, since the total must stay zero

items.explain: With a known total spin of zero, the other particle measured on the same axis is found to spin the opposite way.

items.prompt: A friend says they can text a distant colleague instantly by measuring one of a pair of entangled particles. Why will this not work?

options.label: Nobody can control the outcome of an individual measurement
Entangled particles stop being linked at long distances
The signal arrives but is too weak to read
Phones interfere with the particles

items.explain: Individual measurement outcomes cannot be controlled, so entanglement alone cannot transmit information.

items.prompt: Experiments statistically violated Bell's inequality. What did that tell physicists about entangled particles?

options.label: The particles were secretly sending signals to each other
The experimenters' equipment was faulty
Their correlations cannot be explained by local hidden variables
Einstein's view had been fully confirmed

items.explain: Violating Bell's inequality established that entanglement correlations cannot be explained in terms of local hidden variables.

items.prompt: A pair of gloves is split into two boxes sent far apart; opening one shows which hand the other is. Why is entanglement more than this?

options.label: Gloves are heavier than particles
The boxes could be opened in any order
Entangled particles are always identical copies
Its correlations cannot in general be replicated by classical probability

items.explain: Entanglement is not ordinary correlation: the correlations from an entangled state cannot in general be reproduced by classical probability.

items.prompt: Einstein found entangled behaviour troubling. What did he conclude from it?

options.label: That the accepted formulation of quantum mechanics must be incomplete
That light travels faster than he had thought
That particles have no properties at all
That experiments on pairs should be banned

items.explain: Einstein and others considered the behaviour impossible because it violated local realism, and argued quantum mechanics must therefore be incomplete.

items.prompt: Why do researchers describe entanglement as a resource, much as energy is for machines?

options.label: It can be stored in batteries and sold
It makes particles heavier and easier to move
It reduces the need for any measurement
It makes tasks involving communication and computation possible

items.explain: Just as energy facilitates mechanical operations, entanglement facilitates tasks that involve communication and computation.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Quantum entanglement happens when particles in a group are linked so that the quantum state of any one of them cannot be described apart from the others. This stays true even when the particles are a long way from each other. Entanglement is a core feature of quantum mechanics with no counterpart in classical mechanics, and it sits at the centre of the gap between the two kinds of physics.

paragraphs.heading: Results that match
paragraphs.text: Measure a property such as position, momentum, spin or polarization on entangled particles, and the results can sometimes line up perfectly. Picture a pair made so that their total spin is zero. If one turns out to spin clockwise along some axis, the other, checked on that same axis, spins counterclockwise. Still, entanglement is not the everyday kind of correlation from classical probability. It is better seen as potential correlation that a suitable experiment can turn into real correlation, and its patterns generally cannot be copied by classical probability.

paragraphs.heading: Why it cannot send messages
paragraphs.text: Measuring a particle causes what looks like an irreversible collapse of its wave function, changing the quantum state it started in. With entangled particles, that measurement affects the linked system as a whole. Even so, nobody can choose what any single measurement will show. That is why entanglement can tie together events in far-apart places but cannot carry a message faster than light.

paragraphs.heading: Spooky action at a distance
paragraphs.text: In 1935 Albert Einstein, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen published a thought experiment, now called the EPR paradox, about two systems that interact and then move apart. They argued that quantum mechanics could not then describe each system on its own, so its picture of reality must be incomplete. Einstein thought such behaviour impossible because it broke the local realism view of causality. Soon after, Erwin Schrödinger wrote to Einstein using the German word Verschränkung, which he himself rendered as entanglement. Einstein later dismissed the effect as spooky action at a distance.

paragraphs.heading: Putting it to the test
paragraphs.text: Bell showed that any theory obeying local realism puts an upper limit on how strong correlations can be, and that quantum theory predicts some entangled systems break that limit. This limit, Bell's inequality, can be checked by experiment, beginning with work by Stuart Freedman and John Clauser in 1972, then Alain Aspect in 1982. Tests that measured the polarization or spin of entangled particles at separate places found the inequality broken. That showed the correlations cannot be explained by local hidden variables. In 2022 Aspect, Clauser and Anton Zeilinger shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for experiments with entangled photons.

paragraphs.heading: From the lab to new tools
paragraphs.text: In 1949 Chien-Shiung Wu and Irving Shaknov showed that entangled pairs of the kind EPR imagined could be made in a laboratory. Entanglement has since been shown in electrons, photons, molecules, top quarks and even small diamonds. Physicists treat it as a resource, much as energy is, for tasks in communication and computation. Quantum teleportation, proposed in 1992 using entanglement, was carried out in 1997, and Artur Ekert built a key-sharing protocol called E91 on the breaking of a Bell inequality.
